explanation: push_back copies or moves once and emplace_back constructs in place; there is never a reallocation. With 6 elements the vector is full: push_back and emplace_back throw std::bad_alloc (false / -4) and try_push_back returns nullptr (false), all without constructing anything.

insert(pos, T&&) in the middle move-constructs the last element into the raw slot at end(), move-assigns the elements in between one place right and move-assigns the value into *pos. erase move-assigns the following elements one place left and destroys the (moved-from) last one.

Copy assignment assigns over the 3 elements both have and destroys the target's other 2. Moving an InplaceVector moves each element: its storage is inline, so there is nothing to steal, and the source keeps its 3 (moved-from) elements.
An empty InplaceVector has room for 6 elements but constructs none.
The elements live inside the InplaceVector object.
A full InplaceVector rejects every push without constructing anything; the argument of push_back(T&&) and try_push_back(T&&) is not moved from.
pop_back destroys the last element; its slot is raw storage again and is reused by the next push.
clear destroys each element exactly once.
The destructor destroys exactly the live elements, once each.
emplace_back perfectly forwards its arguments into a single in-place construction.
insert at the front shifts every element; insert at end() just move-constructs; insert into a full vector throws std::bad_alloc (-4) and changes nothing.
Inserting into a full InplaceVector throws std::bad_alloc before touching any element.
insert(pos, const T&) gives the same contents as the move version.
v.insert(pos, v[j]) must insert the value v[j] had before the call, even when the shift moves or overwrites v[j].
Erasing the last element just destroys it; erasing at i move-assigns the size() - 1 - i elements after it, then destroys the last.
erase(first, last) move-assigns the elements after last into place and destroys last - first elements at the end; an empty range does nothing.
The copy constructor copy-constructs each element into the new vector's own storage.
Assigning a longer vector: copy-assign the 2 elements the target has, copy-construct the other 3.
Assigning a shorter vector: copy-assign the common elements, destroy the target's surplus.
v = v leaves v unchanged.
The move constructor move-constructs each element; the source keeps its size, holding moved-from elements, and stays usable.
Move assignment move-assigns the common elements, then move-constructs the rest or destroys the surplus; the source keeps its moved-from elements.
v = std::move(v) leaves v unchanged.
